author: Declaration Desk
title: Qatari mediators float Hormuz-for-blockade trade as US sends a third carrier toward Iran
dek: Regional officials told AP talks have progressed, while Israel is reported to be lobbying for fresh strikes and Gulf states warn against them.
body:
Qatari mediators are trying to build a framework under which Iran would stop attacks in the Strait of Hormuz in return for the United States lifting its blockade of Iranian ports, according to two regional officials quoted by the Associated Press. The officials, who spoke anonymously about classified briefings, said the mediators held two rounds of talks with Iranian officials last week and more are planned this week. Neither Washington nor Tehran has confirmed the framework.

The reports come after US officials said American forces carried out limited "defensive" strikes on Iranian targets near Qeshm Island on Monday, which AP described as appearing limited rather than a return to full hostilities.

## Diplomacy: what each side says

US Vice President JD Vance said on Monday: "We've had a number of good conversations with the Iranians," and that he and President Donald Trump "feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement." He had sent a letter to Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei last week; Trump said it concerned help with "medical supplies and various things", and the White House has given few details.

Rezaei said he had read the letter, had not yet replied, and that "their tone has completely changed", describing that as a good sign, but added that Iran would keep blockading the strait until its conditions, including release of frozen assets, are met, Arab News reported. Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said Iran had agreed a "two-day plan" with Qatari and Pakistani mediators: on day one the US would take a set of measures, and on day two the strait would reopen. The US has not endorsed that plan. Iran also wants guarantees that the US will implement its side, AP reported, noting that the US and Israel have twice attacked Iran during earlier negotiations.

## Military pressure

AP reported that thousands of US troops remain off Iran enforcing the naval blockade, and that a third aircraft carrier and thousands more troops are on their way to the Middle East. It put the cost of the war to US taxpayers at no less than $47 billion.

## Israel and the Gulf

Two regional officials and a third person familiar with the matter told AP that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has pushed for another wave of strikes after the US midterm elections, and is working with senior US officials to persuade Trump to launch a quick but extensive air campaign. One official said Trump did not appear to have decided. A person briefed on a weekend call said Trump would not commit to military action. The Israeli government did not comment, and the White House did not respond directly. AP's sources linked the push to Netanyahu's political position after his bloc lost its parliamentary majority in last week's election.

Other US allies in the region are warning against new strikes, a third regional official told AP, saying they would destabilise the region and could prompt Yemen's Houthis to step up attacks on Saudi Arabia and Red Sea shipping, and draw in Iran-backed militias in Iraq.

## Why it matters for India

The strait normally carries about a fifth of the world's oil and a large share of liquefied natural gas. Oil prices fell sharply on Monday on signs of diplomatic progress, AP reported, and edged up again after the strike reports. For India, which imports most of its crude and a large share of its gas, the price path matters for the rupee, inflation and fuel costs, and Indian seafarers have been among those caught in attacks on shipping in the Gulf.

## What happens next

More Qatari-mediated contacts are expected this week. The US midterm elections are being held on Tuesday (Wednesday morning in India); Trump has said the US would not launch new strikes before the vote. Whether the reported framework turns into an agreement, or the US takes military action afterwards, is undecided on the evidence available.
